===== NEW MESSAGES SINCE YOUR LAST TURN =====
**Codex (QA & Risk · Closer) — Round 1**

MVP slice: ship the smallest end-to-end trust path first: a fully offline deck/card model + one concrete review workflow using one shared, pure SM-2 module. This means the user can create a deck, add cards, launch review for that deck, reveal a card, grade via Again/Hard/Good/Easy, and see a verified session summary, with every grade persisted synchronously before the next card. That is the slice we can build first and still prove the app’s core promise.

Must-have interactions:
- Deck creation/edit (title + archive flag) and quick card add/edit (front/back/note) with keyboard-friendly flow.
- Review launch from a deck list, with empty-state guidance if no due cards.
- Card reveal and four grade taps.
- Immediate persistence on grade (not deferred until session end).
- Interrupt/resume behavior: kill-and-relaunch preserves already-graded cards/schedules, only transient session UI state can be lost.
- Per-deck due badge and due-list filtering driven by the same shared `dueOnOrBefore(today, card)` function from scheduling semantics (single source of truth).
- Session summary with reviewed count, again-rate, elapsed time.

I will not defer this and call it done until this slice is stable: the hardest product risk is day-boundary correctness and persistence integrity, so everything else waits.

Cut list (explicitly not in this slice):
- no all-decks review mode yet (single-deck flow first to reduce failure surface),
- no CSV import/export,
- no reminders/notification permission flows,
- no stats charts,
- no demo-data toggle,
- no subscription cap gating or StoreKit,
- no cloud-sync or future-feature scaffolding.

Validation criteria for consensus:
- Unit tests cover first-review, lapse reset, ease-factor floor at 1.3, and local-calendar boundary including a DST-transition case, all in the pure SM-2 module with no SwiftData/SwiftUI dependencies.
- A manual check proves local-only operation: create deck/cards, review and grade in simulation with airplane mode on/off (no network dependency), and no hangs.
- Force-quit safety check: grade at least one card, relaunch, and verify its new schedule/due date and interval are already stored.
- Local-day truth check: force app-date/time across midnight/travel-like local timezone change and confirm `due` computation and deck due badge remain consistent with what review loads.
- End-to-end workflow check: one full deck session runs from due filter to final summary with empty-state handled cleanly when queue is empty.

Biggest objection I can see is that skipping all-decks/remainder too early might make the app feel smaller, but this is exactly where risk is concentrated. The final output must preserve the explicit statement that this is a staged ship: SM-2 correctness and interruption-safety come first; everything else is additive only after these acceptance checks pass.

**Claude (Product Strategist · Visionary) — Round 1**

Here's my independent take on where the smallest true slice sits, coming at this as the person pushing for the boldest defensible cut, not the safest one.

The whole six-phase paper trail already converged on one sentence: Recall's actual product is "the schedule is never wrong." Everything else — CSV import, stats charts, reminders, the subscription — is packaging around that one fact. So the smallest slice that's actually worth shipping isn't "fewer screens," it's the single moment where a user feels the algorithm earn their trust: create a deck, add a handful of cards, review them today, come back tomorrow, and the due list is exactly right without them having to think about it. If we can't make that moment land, nothing else in the brief matters; if we can, everything else is additive. I'd build the first slice around manufacturing that moment as fast and as convincingly as possible, and defer literally everything that doesn't serve it.

Concretely: the SM-2 module (tested to the standard already locked — first review, lapse reset, ease floor, calendar-day/DST boundary) is not optional scope, it's the entire product, so it ships first and complete, not partially. Around it, the smallest real workflow is deck create/rename/archive, card create/edit with a fast keyboard path, a review session (single deck and all-decks scope, tap-to-reveal, four-button grade, immediate persist before advancing), and an honest end-of-session summary. That's one complete loop, start to finish, and it's the one the phase rules ask for — "one polished workflow over many shallow features." I'd also keep the demo-data toggle in this slice specifically because an empty first-run kills the emotional payoff before it can happen; a user needs to feel the due list work on cards that already have a plausible history, not just cards they typed in thirty seconds ago.

What I'd cut from this immediate slice, deliberately and by name: CSV import/export, the 30-day forecast and daily-history charts, the daily local reminder, and the entire StoreKit subscription/paywall enforcement. None of those are required to prove or feel the core promise — they're valuable, already-specced, and fully non-negotiable for the eventual product, but they're fast-follow, not proof-of-concept. Shipping a hard 3-deck paywall and entitlement plumbing in the very first build risks spending the scarcest resource (build-and-verify attention) on subscription-lapse edge cases before we've even confirmed the review loop itself feels good. Basic Stats (today's due count, retention rate) is cheap enough and reinforcing enough that I'd keep it in-slice; the two charts are the part I'd cut, since they need real multi-week history to be meaningful anyway and a first build won't have that history yet.

The biggest objection to my own position: cutting monetization and CSV/reminders entirely from the first slice means the "smallest slice" isn't actually a shippable v1 against the full product brief — it's a proof-of-concept that a second slice has to complete before this is the real Recall. That's a legitimate risk if "next_steps_small" is meant to define the only build pass rather than the first of several. I think that risk is worth taking anyway, because the alternative — building all six features plus StoreKit in one shot — is exactly the "larger half-built app" the global rules warn against, and it's how SM-2 correctness (the one thing that must be provably right) ends up rushed to make room for a paywall.

The detail I most want preserved into the final output: the validation criterion for this slice can't be "does it compile," it has to be behavioral — create a deck, add cards, review to completion, force-quit mid-session, relaunch, and confirm graded cards kept their new schedule and ungraded cards are still due, exactly as DEC-prompt_contract-002 and DEC-initial_discussion-003 already require. If that single test doesn't pass on the first build, no amount of additional feature scope should be added on top of it.

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 1**

Looking at round 1, both Codex and Claude agree on a lot of the skeleton, but there's real daylight on exactly where the line sits.

**Where they agree:** The SM-2 module ships first and complete — not partial — with the full locked test suite (first-review, lapse-reset, ease-floor, calendar-day/DST boundary), no SwiftData/SwiftUI imports. Deck and card CRUD with fast keyboard-friendly editing is in. The review loop itself — reveal, four-button grade, immediate synchronous persistence before advancing, honest end-of-session summary — is in, and both insist the validation bar is behavioral, not "does it compile": grade cards, force-quit, relaunch, confirm graded cards kept their new schedule and ungraded cards are still due. Both cut CSV import/export, the two stats charts (30-day forecast, daily history), the daily reminder, and the entire StoreKit/subscription paywall from this first slice — none of that is needed to prove the core promise.

**Where they still disagree, three concrete points:**
1. **All-decks review scope** — Codex wants single-deck review only for this slice (fewer failure surfaces to prove first); Claude wants all-decks scope included now, since it's part of "one complete loop."
2. **Demo-data toggle** — Codex cuts it entirely from this slice; Claude wants it kept in, arguing an empty first-run kills the emotional payoff the phase rules ask for ("keep the slice emotionally satisfying").
3. **Basic Stats view** (today's due count + retention rate, not the charts) — Codex cuts all stats from this slice; Claude wants that minimal version kept since it's cheap and reinforces trust.

These aren't cosmetic gaps — they change what "done" means for the first build pass, so this isn't genuine convergence yet.

CONSENSUS: NO

Next round needs to settle: (a) does the first slice include all-decks review or single-deck only, (b) is the demo-data toggle in or out of this slice, and (c) is a minimal Stats view (due count + retention rate, no charts) in or out.

===== YOUR HAT THIS PHASE =====
Come at this as a Product Strategist — your lens is the core problem, who it's for, user value, scope boundaries, and measurable success. And bring the temperament of the Visionary: push the boldest version of the idea and ask what would make this genuinely remarkable, not just adequate. This is your stance for THIS phase only — lean into it and don't be a yes-man.

response:
Codex, I hear the failure-surface argument on single-deck-only, but I think it's actually backwards once you look at what DEC-initial_discussion-005 already locked in: whatever we build has to retain per-card deck identity through the session so a mixed-deck summary can attribute again-rate per deck. That means the data model and the query layer already have to be scope-general — "give me due cards where deck ∈ {X}" — because a single-deck session is just the case where the scope set has one member. If we build a special-cased single-deck-only query now, we're not reducing risk, we're writing throwaway code we'll rip out the moment slice two asks for all-decks review. The actual failure surface you're worried about — the SM-2 day-boundary correctness, the persistence integrity — doesn't change size based on how many decks are in the scope filter. I'd rather spend the review-surface effort proving the query is correct once, generally, than prove a narrower version now and a wider version later. So I'm holding my position here: all-decks in, and I think on reflection it's not even a genuine scope trade, it's just "build the query right the first time."

On demo data, I want to sharpen my argument because I think there's something Codex's own validation criteria actually depends on. Look at the fourth bullet in Codex's validation list — "force app-date/time across midnight/travel-like local timezone change and confirm due computation... remains consistent." That test only works if there's something already scheduled with a real interval to check against. Here's the thing about SM-2: a card graded "Good" on its first review doesn't come due again today, it comes due tomorrow (interval = 1). So a tester who creates a fresh deck, adds three cards, and reviews them once literally cannot observe "the due list is right tomorrow" without either manipulating the system clock or having some cards that already carry a multi-day review history baked in at install time. Demo data isn't a nice-to-have UX polish item here, it's the only way anyone — us verifying the build, or a first-time user — sees the core promise actually pay off inside a single sitting. Without it, "prove the schedule is never wrong" becomes an untestable claim on day one, and the whole point of this slice was to make that provable, not just implemented. I'd go further than my round-1 position, honestly: I don't think demo data is optional polish, I think it's part of the validation infrastructure for this exact slice, badged and deletable exactly as DEC-prompt_contract-003 already specifies. Cutting it doesn't just cost us an emotional beat, it costs us the ability to demo or verify the one thing this whole slice exists to prove.

Where I'll actually move toward Codex is stats. I said "keep it" in round one, but thinking about it harder, I don't think we need a Stats screen — the fourth tab, Swift Charts import, empty/sparse-state design work — for this slice at all, and building a whole screen for two numbers would be exactly the kind of scope Codex is right to be suspicious of. But the two numbers themselves — today's due count and a plain retention percentage — aren't new work, they're already-computed values (due count is the same shared function driving deck badges per DEC-initial_discussion-004, retention is just good+easy over total gradings, which we're already persisting per grade). So my real proposal is: no Stats screen, no navigation entry for it yet, but surface due count and retention rate as a couple of lines on the Decks screen or in a deck detail view, where they cost us a Text view bound to data we already have, not a feature build. That gets us the trust reinforcement without touching the thing Codex is actually worried about, which is new screens with their own empty/sparse/error-state obligations.

So here's where I land: all-decks scope in, because it's free once the model is right and expensive to retrofit; demo data in, because it's the only way to make the day-boundary promise checkable in one sitting instead of asserting it; and stats cut down to two bare numbers with no dedicated screen, which I think fully answers Codex's actual objection (no new UI-state surface) while keeping the slice from feeling like a hollow shell on first launch.
